A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cartesian-3j/cartnn research despite substantial expansion and retitling. Text, equations and tables support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–F are complete and readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original 3BPA accuracy, speed and memory experiments for Cartesian and spherical models, plus numerical tensor-contraction results in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds Cartesian-model results on Matbench Discovery, thermal-conductivity evaluation and molecular-dynamics throughput measurements.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's basis conversions and brief TACE discussion, v2 introduces the TACE universal-potential model family with explicitly added norm-based nonlinear gates and a five-layer, correlation-two architecture (Sections 4.4 and 5.3). The highest-weight ICTP/ICTC principle already appeared in v1; renaming Cartesian-nj is not itself a method change.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates molecular energy and forces on 3BPA. v2 retains its temperature and dihedral subsets while adding inorganic-materials training on OMat24, sAlex and MPtrj, and evaluations of crystal stability and thermal conductivity through Matbench Discovery.

E2.justification: The original NequIP, Allegro and MACE comparisons remain. New materials comparisons include eSEN-30M-OAM, GRACE, MatRIS and other universal potentials (Tables 3 and 9). Table 4 additionally compares inference implementations including NequIP-AOTI-oeq and MACE-cueq; these are reported comparisons, not merely citations.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce OMat24 pretraining and sAlex/MPtrj finetuning schedules, energy/force/stress Huber-loss settings, and F1 and thermal-conductivity metrics. Table 4 adds ASE throughput testing across atom counts and FP64/FP32 precision. These are additional protocols; the PDFs do not establish a changed split for the retained 3BPA experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds exploratory linear-versus-gated TACE comparisons and reports little performance difference between density and average-neighbor normalization (Section 5.3, Table 3 and Appendix C). The gate comparison also changes model depth, limiting causal attribution. The original contraction analysis is retained as Appendix B/Table 7.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly discloses that multiple random seeds were not tested in Tables 1, 2, 5 and 6, while removing v1's assurance of matched random seeds. This changes seed reporting without establishing a reduction in runs. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 2–3 survive numerically unchanged as v2 Tables 5–6. New main Tables 1–2 report results for the alternative Eq. (5) coupling construction. Tables 3–4 and 9 add substantial materials and throughput results, including TACE-v1-OAM-M's F1 of 0.889 and thermal-conductivity error of 0.173. These additions do not establish a same-setting performance gain over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit Cartesian-3j construction using Wigner-3j coefficients and three path matrices (Eq. 5). The original projection construction remains as Appendix A's Eq. (11), with numerical nonidentity acknowledged. The contraction range and dependence observations remain unchanged and empirical; no new proof establishes them.

C1.justification: v2 retains the controlled-comparison claims but adds competitive universal Cartesian potentials as a central contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. v1's broadly pessimistic conclusion about purely Cartesian models becomes a qualified account distinguishing costly direct conversions from practical, specially designed architectures.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of nonlinear interactions benefiting large materials datasets while harming 3BPA extrapolation, and attributes practical limitations partly to missing fused kernels. Sections 5.3–6 and Appendix E also discuss high-rank scalability and competing tensor-product strategies, substantially extending v1's discussion of conversion costs and highest-weight TACE.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D and Table 8 add detailed architecture equations, training hyperparameters, hardware and training time; code availability now lists a standalone cartnn repository. Conversely, v1's executable examples and several 3BPA reproduction details disappear, including the 500-structure split, validation fraction, cutoff, optimizer and loss weights.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against universal materials potentials, acceleration libraries and alternative tensor products, including GRACE, eSEN, cueq/oeq, Gaunt products and matrix products. Much of the original Cartesian-model discussion moves into Section 2; updated titles or publication details for retained references do not constitute new works.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and v1's combined Results section becomes separate Background, Cartesian Framework and Experiments sections. v2 adds dedicated Related Work and Discussion sections plus Appendices A–F, removes tutorial code examples, and renames Cartesian-nj as Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan Coefficients.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a two-column conference layout with redesigned benchmark tables. Original results move into appendix tables, while new materials, throughput and hyperparameter tables are introduced. Added model-type headers, metric-direction markers and bold comparison values also change how results are presented.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical applicability: v1's empirical case centered on 3BPA conversions, while v2 specifies and evaluates universal Cartesian potentials for crystal stability, thermal conductivity and simulation throughput. Its more qualified conclusions better reflect this evidence. Lost 3BPA reproduction details and confounded gate comparisons remain material weaknesses, but the new empirical support and model specification provide a clear overall gain.
